item.title: Regent Hospital's Shahed arrested again in Dhaka
item.description:
Mohammad Shahed, chairman of Regent Group and Regent Hospital, was arrested again on Monday in the ECB Chattar area in Mirpur, Dhaka, over a case filed with Pallabi Police Station.
Cantonment Police Station arrested Shahed and handed him over to Pallabi Police Station.
Shahin, officer-in-charge (OC) of Cantonment Police Station, said: "There was a warrant against him in a case with Pallabi Police Station. We arrested Shahed and handed him over to them."
Hasan Bashir, OC of Pallabi Police Station, said: "There is a warrant against him in a CR case. Cantonment Police Station arrested him based on our request."
Shahed became widely known in 2020 over a scandal involving fraudulent Covid-19 test certificates issued by Regent Hospital.
On July 6, 2020, the Rapid Action Battalion (RAB), led by Executive Magistrate Sarwar Alam, raided Regent Hospital's Uttara and Mirpur offices. The raid found evidence that the hospital had issued Covid-19 certificates without conducting tests and had taken money from patients under false pretences.
On July 7, 2020, RAB sealed off Regent Hospital and its main office on the instructions of the Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS).
A case was filed the same day against Shahed and 16 others at the Uttara West Police Station.
On July 15, 2020, RAB arrested Shahed in Satkhira as he was allegedly attempting to flee to India. He remained in jail for an extended period in multiple cases.
Shahed was released on bail from Dhaka Central Jail on September 4, 2024. A total of 96 cases were filed against him, of which he was convicted in five. He was released after obtaining bail in all the cases.

item.title: Indian police fire tear gas, baton charge exam protesters
item.description:
Indian police fired tear gas and baton-charged protesters in New Delhi Monday as they tried to march on parliament to demand the resignation of the education minister over irregularities in major examinations.
The protesters, mostly young students, ran for cover as police charged at them and fired tear gas shells near Jantar Mantar in the Indian capital.
They are seeking the resignation of Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan over exam irregularities, including question paper leaks and technical glitches.
Thousands of protesters started gathering from early Monday, defying a steady monsoon drizzle and police barricades, marking one of the biggest demonstrations in the capital for five years.
“Our country deserves a government that is bothered about what the young people have to say and is willing to correct its mistakes,” said Sumit Kumar, 18.
“The future belongs to us and not these politicians.”
The protest comes after prominent activist Sonam Wangchuk was forcibly taken to hospital Saturday, bringing an abrupt end to his 20-day hunger strike in support of youths and the satirical Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) movement.
The CJP has won millions of followers on social media since its launch in May, tapping into widespread anger over the country’s education system and unemployment.
“Is this a war zone? Why is the police resorting to tear gas assault on peaceful protesters?” CJP said in a post on X.
“First your govt ignored this protest for a month and now when we are peacefully marching your govt is attacking us. Why?”
The movement is seen as one of the biggest challenges to Hindu-nationalist Prime Minister Narendra Modi since he won his third term in office in 2024.
Despite rapid economic growth, millions of people in the world’s most populous nation still struggle to find stable and well-paying jobs, fueling discontent.
Some 2.2 million aspiring medical students sat for a re-examination under tight security last month after the previous test was scrapped following a question paper leak that triggered widespread outrage.
That came on top of another scandal related to the online marking system of tests taken by nearly two million high school students.
The CJP said two of its leaders met a senior minister Monday and submitted a letter spelling out their demands after the government reached out to them in the morning.
The Internet was cut in parts of central New Delhi on Monday, with police saying they had not given their permission for the protest.
“Any person violating these prohibitory orders shall be liable for prosecution,” Delhi Police said in a statement.
Shubhi Rao, 16, said she had joined the protest to support Wangchuk and demand accountability from the government.
“Prime Minister Narendra Modi has shown himself as someone who isn’t bothered about the youth of this country,” she told AFP.
Modi, in a public address before the start of the monsoon session of parliament, did not mention the protesters.
But Mallikarjun Kharge, a senior leader of the opposition Congress party, brought up the issue in the upper house.
“Thousands of students have gathered at Jantar Mantar. The government is trying to use force, suppress voices, and drive them away,” he said.
Slogans were also shouted inside the lower house by the opposition benches, demanding the resignation of the education minister and justice for students.

item.title: PM: Govt prioritises international labour standards
item.description:
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman on Monday said that his government attaches the highest importance to protecting workers' rights, ensuring a safe working environment, and implementing international labour standards.
The prime minister made this statement when International Labour Organization (ILO) Director-General Gilbert F Houngbo paid a courtesy call on him at his office in the Bangladesh Secretariat here this morning, according to PM’s Assistant Press Secretary Gazi Shahriar Pamir.
At the outset of the meeting, the ILO director-general congratulated Tarique Rahman on assuming office as the head of the government.
Houngbo said that international confidence in Bangladesh had been further strengthened following the assumption of office by a government elected through the direct votes of the people.
In this context, the ILO director general said the ILO is interested in further strengthening its long-standing partnership with Bangladesh and will continue to work closely with the government for the development of the labour sector.
In response, the prime minister thanked the ILO for its continued cooperation and said that his government attaches the highest importance to protecting workers' rights, ensuring a safe working environment, and implementing international labour standards.
The ILO director general also congratulated the Prime Minister on the election of Bangladesh's Foreign Minister Dr Khalilur Rahman as President of the 81st Session of the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA). He described the achievement as an important recognition of Bangladesh's diplomatic capability and credibility in the international arena.
Houngbo also highly praised the present government for achieving other diplomatic successes at the international level within a short period.
During the meeting, the ILO director general said that the Bangladesh government's ongoing labour sector reforms and commitment to implementing international labour standards are being positively recognised globally.
The other areas that came up in discussion during the meeting include workers' protection, skills development, expanding employment opportunities, and developing a skilled workforce to meet the demands of the changing global labour market. They also discussed the progress of Bangladesh's ready-made garment sector, workplace safety, the development of the informal labour market, and Bangladesh's achievements in implementing international labour standards.
Both sides stressed the importance of strengthening cooperation between the government and the ILO to further advance the ongoing labour sector reform initiatives.
They also exchanged views on ensuring the rights and welfare of migrant workers, establishing a safe and orderly migration system, and further strengthening cooperation in enhancing the skills of overseas-bound workers.
During the meeting, Tarique Rahman reiterated his government's commitment to ensuring a worker-friendly and sustainable working environment.
Besides, the ILO director-general expressed his commitment to further expanding the organisation's existing cooperation with Bangladesh and working jointly for the development of the country's labour sector.
Labour and Employment Minister Ariful Haque Chowdhury, Prime Minister’s Adviser Mahdi Amin, and Secretary to the Labour and Employment Ministry Md Abdur Rahman Tarafder, Director General (UN Wing) at the Foreign Affairs Ministry Md Kamruzzaman, ILO Country Director in Bangladesh, Max Tuñón and Senior Adviser to the ILO Director-General at the ILO Headquarters in Geneva, Hitomi Nakagome were present at the meeting.

item.title: Gas supply to remain suspended in several Dhaka areas Tuesday
item.description:
Gas supply will remain suspended for eight hours in several areas of Dhaka on Tuesday as Titas Gas Transmission and Distribution Company Limited is set to carry out pipeline replacement work.
According to a notice issued by the company on Monday, gas supply will remain shut from 12pm to 8pm in the Free School Street, Bhuter Goli, Kitchen Road, Al Amin Road and Kathalbagan areas.
The suspension will affect both residential and commercial consumers, it said.
Titas Gas said the disruption is necessary to replace old leaking distribution pipelines and service lines in the Free School Street, Hatirpool, Pukurpar and Dhanmondi areas.
The company also warned that consumers in surrounding areas may experience low gas pressure during the maintenance work.
It apologised for the temporary inconvenience to be caused to customers and sought their cooperation during the scheduled maintenance.

item.title: When the rain, the runoff, and the tide arrive together
item.description:
On the night of July 4, 2025, the Guadalupe River in Texas Hill Country rose about 26 feet in 45 minutes. Camp Mystic, a girls' summer camp on its banks, lost 27 campers, counselors, and its director before dawn. More than 135 people died across the region in that single flood, according to state investigative findings.
What made the event so lethal was not simply how much rain fell. The National Weather Service's own warnings that night cited rainfall rates climbing to several inches an hour, a pace that turned a river into a wall of water before most people even understood a flood was underway.
This is the point that gets lost in most conversations about flooding, in Texas and in Bangladesh alike. The number that matters most in the changing climate is often not the total rainfall for the day, but how fast it arrives.
A given volume of rain spread over 12 hours is manageable. The same volume in 90 minutes can be fatal. Chittagong found this out on its own terms this July, when the city recorded about 410 millimetres of rain in 24 hours, according to a Dhaka Tribune report, the heaviest single-day total the port city had seen in 42 years.
The rain fell hardest while the Karnaphuli River was at high tide, and while runoff from the surrounding hills poured into a drainage network already at its limit.
A city I did not expect to see this in
I grew up in Comilla, and waterlogging is not something I remember from my childhood there. A hard rain meant wet streets that dried out again by the next day. That is no longer true. Comilla now floods most summers, sometimes badly enough that students have had to reach their exam centres by boat.
Comilla has no hills to cut and no tide to fight. What it has, like dozens of other urbanizing cities across Bangladesh and beyond, is a much less dramatic but equally potent sequence: Canal margins and low channels lost to construction, drains left uncleared for years, and a habit, shared by households, markets, and construction sites alike, of treating the nearest drain as the easiest place to get rid of waste.
None of that needed a hill or a coastline. It only needed disregard for the environment and indifferent authorities.
Two cities, two different problems
Dhaka and Chittagong show the same underlying pattern at a larger, more studied scale, each with its own mechanism layered on top.
Dhaka's story is mostly about disappearing land. According to a study on canal encroachment in Dhaka, the city has lost roughly 60% of its wetlands and 65% of its canals over the past 30 years, paved over as construction spread.
Retention ponds that once held monsoon runoff have shrunk sharply in the areas where records exist. That is a loss of natural capacity to absorb water, separate from anything happening in the pipes.
The piped network is its own weak point. A Daily Star investigation found that Dhaka's main drainage authority maintains roughly 370 kilometres of storm drainage pipe, covering only about a fifth of the city's 400 square kilometre area, with seven different agencies each looking after their own section and little coordination between them.
So even where canals are intact, the underground system meant to feed them is often undersized, aging, or simply absent.
Chittagong has, or used to have, a hilly terrain and sits next to a coastline, a perfect combination for compound flooding where bidirectional flow coming from the sea and the land overwhelms the natural and built drainage infrastructure.
Chittagong has also historically seen heavier monsoon rain because of its proximity to the sea. When a hillside is cut for construction, it destroys a delicate hydrologic balance. As in Dhaka, loss of natural drainage to land grabbing compounds the strain on what remains of the natural drainage pattern.
According to a 2023 Daily Star report, the city's own drainage authority now counts 56 canals where 72 once existed, and green space has fallen below 15% of the city's land. Underground drainage fares no better. A recent engineering study found that large parts of the city have no properly connected underground network at all, which means canal restoration alone will not solve the problem even where it succeeds.
Underneath both cities' specific drivers of waterlogging sits a simpler failure that needs no special geography to operate: Neglect.
Drains and canals that are not regularly cleared silt up regardless of how well they were designed, and clearing them depends on maintenance schedules and budgets that routinely lose out to flashier priorities.
An ordinary afternoon shower is often enough to expose a canal that has not been desilted in years, or a drain choked with waste that residents and businesses put there themselves.
This pattern is not confined to Dhaka and Chittagong, or even to Bangladesh.
Wetlands, floodplains, and canal margins disappear first precisely because they look empty between storms. Each time this happens, in any city following the same sequence, the next flood has less capacity to work with than the one before it.
Plans that stop keeping up
Dhaka's current drainage plan, drafted by WASA in 2015, assumed 40% of rainfall would soak naturally into the ground, and its pumping stations were sized to match. That was a reasonable estimate at the time, according to an urban planner quoted in a July 2026 Daily Star report.
As concrete replaced open soil across the city in the years since, actual infiltration fell well below that number, and the plan was never revised. The same report notes that the city's pumps can now handle only about 40% of the current load.
Chittagong's plan is older and carries a different kind of stale assumption. Its Storm Water Drainage and Flood Control Master Plan was drafted between 1993 and 1995. One specific flaw stands out: According to a paper in the Journal of Bangladesh Institute of Planners, drain widths were fixed at 2 to 3 feet regardless of whether the road above them was 20 feet or 60 feet wide, so as development scaled up around them, the drains never did.
Hill cutting, meanwhile, is banned under a separate national law, the Environment Conservation Act of 1995, but enforcement has been too weak to stop it.
Spending has not been the constraint
Chittagong's experience argues against the idea that money is the missing piece. According to a recent statement from the finance minister, four major flood-mitigation projects have been running for close to a decade, with roughly Tk 14,400 crore allocated and about Tk 10,400 crore of it already spent.
A separate Daily Star report found that the largest single project, covering 36 canals, has seen its cost rise from about Tk 5,600 crore to roughly Tk 8,600 crore, with its deadline pushed from 2020 to 2026. Over that same period, according to the same report, the city has lost 47 of its original 104 canals to encroachment and sedimentation.
Money spent building fixed infrastructure to an unrevised design, without enforcement, coordination, or updated assumptions behind it, buys less every year the city keeps changing. A bigger budget applied to the same static approach does not fix that problem. It just makes it more expensive.
What this argues for
None of this argues against having a master plan. It argues against treating one as a document written once and left alone for 20 years.
A better version is a living plan: Built and updated at the scale of individual drainage basins, with lessons from each basin carried into the next. In practice, that means:
Jasim Imran is Professor in the Department of Civil and Environmental Engineering at the University of South Carolina. The opinions expressed here are the author's own. Figures cited in this piece were drawn from publicly available sources.

item.title: Stakeholders call for sustainable financing to prevent child drowning
item.description:
Speakers at a stakeholder dialogue on Sunday called for sustainable financing and stronger multi-stakeholder collaboration to strengthen child drowning prevention efforts in Bangladesh.
They stressed that, alongside government funding, greater participation from the private sector, local government institutions, development partners, the media and other stakeholders is essential to ensure the long-term sustainability of drowning prevention initiatives.
The dialogue, titled "Prevention of Child Drowning and Sustainable Financing for Child Protection," was held at The Daily Star Centre in Dhaka. It was organised by Somashte Media Communication and Development Foundation, with support from the Global Health Advocacy Incubator (GHAI).
The event brought together government officials, representatives from the private sector, development partners, media professionals and public health experts.
Delivering the welcome address, Mir Masruruzzaman, executive director of Somashte, said an average of 40 children die from drowning every day in Bangladesh, yet the issue receives inadequate attention.
He said most child drowning incidents occur between 9am and 2pm, when caregivers are often occupied with work, leaving children without adequate supervision.
"A child can drown not only in large water bodies but also in shallow water. Ensuring safe supervision is therefore critical to preventing drowning," he said.
Rezaul Haque, Somashte's director of research and communications, presented an overview of drowning deaths in Bangladesh, the national strategy, the current financing framework and the potential role of stakeholders, including the private sector.
He said the national action plan aims to reduce drowning deaths by 50% by 2030. More than 18,000 people currently die from drowning each year. However, he said clearer funding sources, dedicated budget lines and expenditure-tracking mechanisms are needed to implement the plan effectively.
The presentation highlighted the Integrated Community-Based Childcare and SwimSafe (ICBC) project, which has provided childcare services, swimming lessons, CPR training, safe rescue education, water safety measures and awareness activities in 16 districts. The project's second phase is currently awaiting approval.
Professor Dr Kazi Maruful Islam of the Department of Development Studies at the University of Dhaka said drowning prevention should be viewed as a continuous social service rather than a project. He emphasised integrating such initiatives into existing local government structures.
Jamira Shabnam, deputy secretary of the Finance Division, called for coordinated initiatives prioritising high-risk areas. She said the central government, local government institutions and other stakeholders all have important roles to play in preventing drowning.
Reaz Ahmad, editor of Dhaka Tribune, said existing projects should be expanded rather than discontinued. He stressed the need for risk-based planning and data-driven management of drowning prevention efforts.
Azharul Haque Azad, managing director of Sadakalo, said raising public awareness about drowning is crucial. He added that collaboration between the media and business organisations could help build large-scale social initiatives.
Zahidul Islam Sajal, head of public communications at Nagad, said the social importance and measurable impact of drowning prevention must be clearly communicated to encourage greater private sector participation.
"Corporate organisations need to clearly understand both the importance of the issue and the opportunities for engagement," he said, adding that digital platforms also offer significant potential for public engagement and fundraising.
Sohrab Hasan, editor of Charcha.com, stressed the need to strengthen public awareness and community initiatives, particularly at the local level.
Media representatives, including Kajal Ghosh of Manab Zamin, Rabeya Baby of The Daily Ittefaq, Partha Shankar Saha of Prothom Alo, Zahid Rahman of Channel i and Saiduzzaman Rowshan of Agami Shomoy, discussed the role of the media in raising awareness and promoting policy attention to drowning prevention.
Sazia Afrin, communications manager at Synergos, said community acceptance of the ICBC project has been strong.
"The challenge now is ensuring these activities continue not only during the project period but also after it ends," she said.
Speakers concluded that while government funding should remain the primary source of financing, long-term sustainability will require complementary support from the private sector, corporate social responsibility initiatives, development partners and local stakeholders.
They also called for dedicated budget allocations across relevant ministries, stronger local government involvement, greater private sector participation and a transparent reporting mechanism to support effective implementation of drowning prevention initiatives.

item.title: PM orders transparent rollout of Family Card program
item.description:
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman on Monday instructed the authorities concerned to ensure the Family Card programme is implemented through a transparent process, with a reliable database to accurately identify genuine beneficiaries.
He issued the directives during a meeting on the gradual expansion and implementation strategy of the nationwide Family Card programme at the Cabinet Division in the Bangladesh Secretariat, according to a press release issued by the Prime Minister's Press Wing.
The meeting reviewed the progress of the Family Card program, one of the key pledges in the BNP's election manifesto, and discussed a roadmap for its gradual expansion across the country.
The prime minister emphasised the need for a practical implementation plan, effective coordination among all relevant ministries and agencies, and the best possible use of modern technology to ensure the programme is rolled out smoothly nationwide.
He also stressed the importance of establishing a credible and acceptable database so that the benefits of the Family Card programme reach the actual recipients effectively, accurately, and transparently.
Tarique Rahman asked the authorities to maintain the highest standards of transparency and accountability at every stage of data collection, verification, and beneficiary selection.
Social Welfare Minister Dr AZM Zahid Hossain, State Minister for Social Welfare Farzana Sharmin, Prime Minister's Adviser Mahdi Amin, Principal Secretary ABM Abdus Sattar, Chief SDG Coordinator at the Prime Minister's Office Prof Dr SM Abdul Awal, BNP National Executive Committee’s Special Secretary Belayet Hossain Mridha, and senior officials from the relevant ministries and agencies attended the meeting.

item.title: Rashed Khan appointed as political assistant to PM
item.description:
Md Rashed Khan has been appointed political assistant to Prime Minister Tarique Rahman on a contractual basis, with the status of secretary, according to a notification issued by the Ministry of Public Administration on Sunday.
The appointment is conditional on Rashed Khan severing ties with any other profession, business, or government, semi-government, or private institution or entity.
He will serve from the date of joining until the end of the prime minister's tenure, or until the prime minister withdraws consent, whichever comes first, the notification said.
Other terms and conditions of the appointment will be determined through a separate contract.
Rashed Khan first gained national prominence as joint convener of the Bangladesh Chhatra Odhikar Parishad, which led the 2018 quota reform movement, while he was a student at the University of Dhaka.

item.title: Andy Burnham set to take over as new British PM
item.description:
Andy Burnham will Monday become Britain’s sixth prime minister to move into Downing Street since 2016, with an in-tray overflowing with challenges and little time to make his mark.
The new leader takes over from the unpopular Keir Starmer just two years after the outgoing prime minister led Labour to power in a landslide election victory after 14 years of Conservative rule.
After being asked by King Charles III to form the next government, Burnham, 56, is due to make his first speech Monday outside 10 Downing Street shortly after Starmer has said his farewells.
In an interview with The Times published late Sunday, Burnham set out his ambition for change, saying he wanted to draw a line under a decade of political turmoil.
“What we’ve been doing hasn’t been working. That’s the way I see it,” he said.
“I am going to try and do things in a different way.”
In his first speech he was to acknowledge he feels “acutely conscious” of the need for a more stable brand of politics, as he becomes the sixth new prime minister in the last 10 years.
Burnham will set out “priorities for restoring confidence in government and giving Britain more breathing room” amid the cost-of-living crisis, his team said.
Delivering growth and devolving power to regional communities are also expected to feature.
An announcement on his senior cabinet appointments was also expected on Monday with all eyes on who will replace Rachel Reeves as finance minister.
The former mayor of Greater Manchester, nicknamed the “King of the North,” has been parachuted in by the Labour Party, after Starmer resigned last month, with MPs viewing him as the party’s best chance of reining in Nigel Farage’s anti-immigration Reform UK party.
Deputy Labour Party leader Lucy Powell said Sunday Burnham’s mayoral experience away from the London centre of government meant he understood the “bigger, bolder measures” needed to deliver on Labour’s election manifesto promises.
Among Burnham’s most urgent challenges will be a tepid economy, high government borrowing costs, a ballooning welfare bill and irregular migrants arriving in small boats that have fueled support for Reform.
Unpredictable energy prices due to the US-Iran war and a volatile American president in Donald Trump also threaten to buffet his premiership.
Burnham told The Times he would take a “different approach to public spending, and to running the economy -- more focused on early investment, early intervention, setting people up for success, and much less paying for failure.”
He promised “early moves to help” with the cost of living, saying that while campaigning he heard the “pressure people feel around their finances.”
Starmer announced that he would resign as prime minister and Labour Party leader in late June after a string of scandals, missteps and policy U-turns blighted his leadership.
But Burnham, who only returned as a member of parliament four weeks ago, has little room to manoeuvre amid sluggish economic growth, high public debt and strict financial rules requiring him to balance government spending against tax revenue.
Monday’s handover will begin with Starmer visiting Buckingham Palace to formally tender his resignation to the king before making a brief statement outside 10 Downing Street.
Burnham will then make his own trip to Buckingham Palace, before his first speech as prime minister which will be a moment of “reflection and resolution,” he will say, stressing Britain must be honest about the challenges it faces.
Burnham was an MP between 2001 and 2017, serving as a minister the governments of Tony Blair and Gordon Brown.
He has since reinvented himself as a man of the people, melding a relaxed, folksy style with slick social media videos.
But he has only three years to turn things around, with Reform tipped in polls to win the next general election expected in 2029.
Burnham told supporters on Friday his Labour takeover was the “last chance” for the party to get things right.
Critics have accused Starmer’s government of being under-prepared for power when he was elected in July 2024.
Burnham has insisted he has a “plan.”
But his swift “coronation” as Labour leader has raised questions on how he will achieve his aims.
His first policy announcement came on Saturday when he scrapped Starmer’s flagship nationwide digital ID scheme, estimated to cost £1.8 billion over three years.
A spokesperson said the time and resources would be diverted “to where it’s most needed, such as helping with the cost of living.”

item.title: Mozaffar Hossain’s trial under military law: Home Minister
item.description:
Home Minister Salahuddin Ahmed has said that the trial of Major (retd) Mozaffar Hossain, an accused in the assassination case of the martyred President Ziaur Rahman, will be conducted under military law through a general court martial.

He made the remarks on Monday afternoon while responding to questions from newspersons at a press conference held at Shaheed Captain Ashraf Hall in Pilkhana, Dhaka.

Earlier, he visited the Border Guard Bangladesh (BGB) headquarters.

“Major (retd) Mozaffar Hossain has been arrested. His other associates were tried by a military court at the time, and certain observations were recorded in those proceedings. He had remained a fugitive for many years in a neighbouring country under a different identity. Acting on intelligence information, we arrested him and handed him over to the Bangladesh Army for trial under military law,” the home minister said.

Stating that Mozaffar’s trial will be ensured through a general court martial, Salahuddin Ahmed further said, “If the judgment against those convicted in the assassination case of the martyred President Ziaur Rahman contains any observations relating to him, the general court martial will consider those.”

Asked whether any proceedings would also be initiated against him under civil law, the home minister said it would be examined at a later stage whether such action would be legally permissible.

“Not at this stage. The same individual cannot be tried twice under two different legal frameworks for the same offence,” he remarked.

On 15 July, the Detective Branch (DB) announced the arrest of Major (retd) Mozaffar Hossain, 77, who had allegedly remained a fugitive for 45 years in connection with the assassination of former President Ziaur Rahman.

Ziaur Rahman assassination: Mozaffar's role and 45 years in hiding

He was arrested from a residence in Banani, Dhaka, on the night of 15 July and was handed over to the military police at Dhaka Cantonment the following day.

Barbed-wire fence along Myanmar border

Responding to a question on the construction of a barbed-wire fence along the Bangladesh–Myanmar border, Home Minister Salahuddin Ahmed said, “The Myanmar border has become extremely risky for Bangladesh for a number of reasons. Clashes frequently occur between the Myanmar military and the Arakan Army along the border. In addition, several armed insurgent groups, including the Rohingya Solidarity Organisation (RSO) and the Arakan Rohingya Salvation Army (ARSA), remain active there. The impact of their internal conflicts often spills over into Bangladesh's border areas.”

Referring to the deteriorating security situation, he said it had contributed to an increase in cross-border narcotics trafficking and that Bangladeshi citizens had, on occasion, been killed or injured in cross-border exchanges of fire.

Taking these issues into account, he said, the government is considering a proposal to construct 109 kilometres of barbed-wire fencing along the Myanmar border.

The government is yet to make a final decision, he added.

Responding to another question on the government's measures to prevent landmine-related incidents along the border, Salahuddin Ahmed said the necessary mine-detection equipment had already been procured and supplied to the Border Guard Bangladesh (BGB). BGB personnel are using the equipment to help prevent accidents caused by landmine explosions.

'Push-ins' from India

Asked about alleged "push-ins" from India, the home minister said, "The government has not allowed a single person to be illegally pushed into Bangladesh. With the support of the BGB and residents of the border areas, we have so far been able to prevent such attempts successfully. There have been a small number of instances of illegal entry, but the number is not significant. Those who entered the country illegally have been dealt with in accordance with the law. However, we have not allowed any push-ins."

DB hands over detained former army officer Mozaffar Hossain to the Army

He added that the newly elected government in West Bengal had sought to present the issue differently for its own political agenda, but Bangladesh had no comment on that.

"We will engage with the Government of India at the central level on this matter. If any Bangladeshi nationals are residing in India, a list must be sent through the Ministry of Foreign Affairs in accordance with the prescribed procedures. Bangladesh will verify their citizenship, and if their nationality is confirmed, they will be repatriated through the appropriate legal process. No one else will be accepted," he stated.

Salahuddin Ahmed also said it had been decided to make more effective use of the BGB's dog squad.

He noted that the government's recently enacted modern and robust narcotics control law includes provisions for the deployment of dog squads.

However, he said, training additional specialist dog units would take time, and until then, the existing BGB dog squads would continue to be utilised.

The home minister further said that a number of decisions had been taken to strengthen the BGB, including increasing its human resources and procuring additional vehicles, modern equipment and weapons.

He also announced plans to further expand and reinforce the “Aid to Civil Power” programme.

item.title: TOP SHOTS (20 July 2026)
Andy Burnham set to become UK PM
item.description:
BRITAIN-POLITICS

Andy Burnham will Monday become Britain's sixth prime minister to move into Downing Street since 2016, with an in-tray overflowing with challenges and little time to make his mark.

The new leader takes over from the unpopular Keir Starmer just two years after the outgoing prime minister led Labour to power in a landslide election victory after 14 years of Conservative rule.

After being asked by King Charles III to form the next government, Burnham, 56, is due to make his first speech Monday outside 10 Downing Street shortly after Starmer has said his farewells.

In an interview with The Times published late Sunday, Burnham set out his ambition for change, saying he wanted to draw a line under a decade of political turmoil.

"What we've been doing hasn't been working. That's the way I see it," he said.

"I am going to try and do things in a different way."

In his first speech he was to acknowledge he feels "acutely conscious" of the need for a more stable brand of politics, as he becomes the sixth new prime minister in the last 10 years.

Burnham will set out "priorities for restoring confidence in government and giving Britain more breathing room" amid the cost-of-living crisis, his team said.

Delivering growth and devolving power to regional communities are also expected to feature.

An announcement on his senior cabinet appointments was also expected on Monday with all eyes on who will replace Rachel Reeves as finance minister.

The former mayor of Greater Manchester, nicknamed the "King of the North", has been parachuted in by the Labour Party, after Starmer resigned last month, with MPs viewing him as the party's best chance of reining in Nigel Farage's anti-immigration Reform UK party.

''Bigger, bolder''

Deputy Labour Party leader Lucy Powell said Sunday Burnham''s mayoral experience away from the London centre of government meant he understood the "bigger, bolder measures" needed to deliver on Labour's election manifesto promises.

Among Burnham's most urgent challenges will be a tepid economy, high government borrowing costs, a ballooning welfare bill and irregular migrants arriving in small boats that have fuelled support for Reform.
Unpredictable energy prices due to the US-Iran war and a volatile American president in Donald Trump also threaten to buffet his premiership.

Burnham told The Times he would take a "different approach to public spending, and to running the economy -- more focused on early investment, early intervention, setting people up for success, and much less paying for failure."

He promised "early moves to help" with the cost of living, saying that while campaigning he heard the "pressure people feel around their finances".

Starmer announced that he would resign as prime minister and Labour Party leader in late June after a string of scandals, missteps and policy U-turns blighted his leadership.

But Burnham, who only returned as a member of parliament four weeks ago, has little room to manoeuvre amid sluggish economic growth, high public debt and strict financial rules requiring him to balance government spending against tax revenue.

Monday's handover will begin with Starmer visiting Buckingham Palace to formally tender his resignation to the king, after making a brief statement outside 10 Downing Street.

Burnham will then make his own trip to Buckingham Palace, before his first speech as prime minister which will be a moment of "reflection and resolution," he will say, stressing Britain must be honest about the challenges it faces.

''Last chance''

Burnham was an MP between 2001 and 2017, serving as a minister the governments of Tony Blair and Gordon Brown.

He has since reinvented himself as a man of the people, melding a relaxed, folksy style with slick social media videos.

But he has only three years to turn things around, with Reform tipped in polls to win the next general election expected in 2029.

Burnham told supporters on Friday his Labour takeover was the "last chance" for the party to get things right.

Critics have accused Starmer's government of being under-prepared for power when he was elected in July 2024.

Burnham has insisted he has a "plan".

But his swift "coronation" as Labour leader has raised questions on how he will achieve his aims.

His first policy announcement came on Saturday when he scrapped Starmer's flagship nationwide digital ID scheme, estimated to cost £1.8 billion over three years.

A spokesperson said the time and resources would be diverted "to where it's most needed, such as helping with the cost of living".

item.title: Spain: Control, composure, champions
item.description:
Four years ago, Argentina rode out countless storms en route to the title, eventually defeating France 4-2 on penalties after a breathtaking 3-3 draw in the final. This year’s showpiece in New York New Jersey saw La Albiceleste cede the throne to Spain, who claimed the crown by imposing order and maintaining constant control.
Spain capped their North American campaign with a display of technical and tactical excellence in the final, shutting down the opposition attack more effectively than ever. After stifling France and their fearsome forwards in a 2-0 semi-final win, the European champions turned their attention to Lionel Messi & Co, who became the latest victims of La Roja’s relentless march.
The Argentines had scored at least two goals in each of their previous matches, but this time they were uncharacteristically quiet. Lionel Scaloni’s men did not muster a single shot on target in 120 minutes, their only attempts coming in extra time and never truly troubling Unai Simon in the Spain goal.
“We’ve got a wonderful team,” said right-back Pedro Porro, speaking exclusively with FIFA. “We put up a great fight, right from the first minute. We’ve done that from the start against Cabo Verde, when we kept possession and created chances, but they just didn’t go in.”
In a match where the stakes could not have been any higher, Spain never lost their way or their focus. They controlled the tempo without ever losing their composure, just as they had in their 1-0 win over Portugal in the last 16 and a 2-1 triumph over Belgium in the quarters, when the winning goal was slow to materialise. Aside from their technical dominance, the Spanish stayed remarkably calm at a time when doubt could easily have set in.
“We stayed true to our style, I think that’s obvious,” continued Porro.
Luis de la Fuente's side had laid the foundations for their North American campaign at EURO 2024 in Germany, but this time round their style of play also relied on lightning-fast counter-attacks with jet-heeled wingers Lamine Yamal and Nico Williams. They were perhaps more direct two years ago and were more willing to engage in open matches, conceding four goals in their four knockout matches.
In North America, however, they remarkably shipped just a solitary goal, scored by Belgium’s Charles De Ketelaere, an unprecedented feat in the history of the tournament.
What has certainly changed over the past two years is the influence of the team’s metronome Rodri, winner of the adidas Golden Ball for the tournament’s best player. Holding the FIFA World Cup™ Trophy in his arms, the midfield maestro explained to FIFA how Spain were able to dominate all of their opponents.
“I think we’re the team that handles the most game situations,” he said. “Pressing, possession, counter-attacks, set pieces… I think that, in every aspect of football, Spain are the team that can control the game the best.”
When Rodri steps up the pace, so do Spain. When he chooses to disrupt the opposition’s rhythm, the whole team follows suit with remarkable composure, without ever losing their shape. La Roja’s 2026 vintage is not content to simply dominate possession, however, as they also dictate what their opponents do when they have the ball.
The newly crowned world champions were perhaps slightly less spectacular than they were two years ago, but this time they made control their greatest strength.
“We knew we wouldn’t conceded a lot of goals,” admitted Porro. “But we also knew that we had what it took to compete with anyone. In the end, we were rewarded with a wonderful prize.”
Four years ago, it was Argentina who emerged victorious from a storm in Qatar. This year, it was Spain who lifted the trophy by bringing a sense of calm back to proceedings. In a tournament that always seemed destined to be dominated by the teams with the strongest attacks, it was ultimately La Roja who carved out a path to the very top of the global game.
