item.title: A year on, Milestone children still fear the sound of planes
item.description:
Nearly a year after a Bangladesh Air Force training aircraft crashed into Milestone School and College in Uttara, killing 36 people, including 28 students, the classrooms have reopened, examinations have resumed and lessons continue.
But for many children who survived the country’s deadliest aviation disaster on a school campus, recovery remains far from complete.
What was once a familiar sound has become a trigger.
Before the crash, students would often rush to classroom balconies whenever an aircraft flew overhead, watching it disappear into the sky.
Today, many instinctively freeze or look for cover when they hear the roar of an engine.
For them, the sound no longer represents curiosity, it recalls the afternoon of July 21, 2025.
A visit by Dhaka Tribune to the Diyabari campus found the damaged Haider Ali Academic Building still abandoned behind a corrugated tin fence.
The upper floors facing the main road have been demolished, while the surrounding classrooms that once accommodated students from Classes I to VIII remain vacant.
The building has become a daily reminder of the tragedy for students who pass it on their way to class.
Muktadir, now a Class VI student, was inside the building when the aircraft crashed.
He recalled that teachers managed to evacuate students amid the chaos, but said the experience continues to shape his life.
“We used to enjoy watching planes from school,” he told Dhaka Tribune.
“Now I’m frightened whenever I hear one.”
His voice broke as he remembered classmates who never returned and friends who later transferred to other schools.
Another student, Wasifia Zafrin, now in Class VII, said she still thinks about classmates who died in the disaster and admitted that every aircraft passing overhead revives memories of that day.
The emotional scars remain visible beyond the classroom.
Some students who suffered severe burns still do not attend regular classes, appearing only for examinations.
Among them is Samia Akhter, whose face and hand were badly burned in the crash.
Her mother, Shiuli Akter, said Samia continues to undergo laser treatment and will require reconstructive plastic surgery in the future.
“She cannot stay in the sun and still doesn’t attend classes regularly,” she said.
“She only comes for examinations.”
Parents say the abandoned building itself continues to reinforce children’s fears and have urged the authorities to complete its demolition and redevelopment as quickly as possible.
School authorities acknowledge that the trauma persists.
Public Relations Officer Shah Bulbul said teachers continue to provide psychological counselling and recently launched a healing initiative titled “You Are Immortal Among the Green,” during which 35 saplings were planted in memory of the students and teachers who lost their lives.
School in-charge Akram Hossain said counselling sessions remain part of regular classroom activities, while students still recovering physically are given additional support during examinations.
The anniversary also revives broader questions about aviation safety.
A government investigation concluded that pilot error caused the crash but also found that the school building failed to comply with RAJUK’s building code, having only one staircase instead of the required three -- an architectural deficiency investigators believe contributed to the death toll.
Following the tragedy, the Civil Aviation Authority of Bangladesh recommended inspections of buildings within a 15-kilometre radius of Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport.
Air Commodore Md Noor-e-Alam told Dhaka Tribune that inspections are under way in coordination with the Ministry of Land and RAJUK, although implementation has taken longer than expected.
For investigators, the crash has become a case study in aviation safety and urban planning.
For Milestone’s children, however, it remains something far more personal.
A year later, the classrooms are open again -- but for many of those who survived, the sound of an aircraft still carries them back to the afternoon when childhood was interrupted in an instant.

item.title: For one mother, school never ended
item.description:
Every afternoon, when schools begin to empty across Dhaka, Mahmuda Akhter finds herself looking toward the door.
For a fleeting moment, she still believes her 10-year-old son, Omair Noor Asfiq, will return home with his schoolbag on his shoulder, smiling as he always did after class.
Then reality returns.
Asfiq was among the 28 students killed when a Bangladesh Air Force FT-7 BGI training aircraft crashed into Milestone School and College on July 21 last year.
One year later, the routines of motherhood remain.
The child does not.
“I still feel it’s time to go and bring him home from school,” Mahmuda told Dhaka Tribune.
“Sometimes I unknowingly start getting ready. Then I remember he isn’t coming back.”
For Mahmuda, time has remained suspended on the morning she prepared breakfast, packed her son’s school bag and watched him leave for class.
It was an ordinary day.
Asfiq, a Class III student, was known for finishing his homework early and insisting on sitting in the front row.
That morning, instead of walking with his mother as he often had in the past, he rode to school on his uncle’s motorcycle.
His mother planned to take his afternoon tiffin later.
Instead, she sent it with another family member.
It is a decision she still struggles to forgive herself for.
“My sister-in-law told me she saw him while giving him his lunch because he was sitting in the front,” she said.
“I keep asking myself why I didn’t go that day. I never got to see my son one last time.”
Shortly after noon, panic spread through the neighbourhood.
Her brother-in-law, who worked at Milestone, called after failing to locate Asfiq following the crash.
Mahmuda rushed barefoot to the school.
Parents crowded the gates, desperate for information.
She searched classrooms, medical camps and every corner of the campus, convinced her son was alive.
“I never imagined I would lose him,” she said. “I believed I would find him.”
Relatives tried to shield her from the truth, telling her Asfiq had suffered only minor injuries and was being treated.
Hours later, his body came home.
“When they laid him on the bed, his face was red from the fire,” she recalled. “As a mother, there are no words to describe that pain.”
One memory torments her more than any other.
Asfiq had been born with a heart condition and was unusually sensitive to loud sounds.
“He would become frightened even if a balloon burst,” she said. “I never took him to birthday parties because doctors told me to keep him away from loud noise.”
“Yet my son died in the loudest moment of his life.”
Today, almost everything that belonged to Asfiq remains exactly where he left it.
His books, homework, clothes and belongings have been carefully preserved.
“I have everything my son used,” Mahmuda said quietly.
“Everything except my son.”
His younger sister still grows up surrounded by stories he never had the chance to fulfil.
He had promised that when he grew older and bought a motorcycle, he would take her to school every day so their mother would no longer have to walk.
That promise now exists only in memory.
Even after a year, Mahmuda says the family’s search for accountability remains incomplete.
“We still haven’t received justice,” she said.
“Governments have changed, but nothing has changed for us. Everyone has moved on. A mother cannot.”
For the rest of the city, July 21 has become an anniversary.
For Mahmuda Akhter, it returns every afternoon -- when the school bell rings, when children walk home with their parents, and when instinct still tells her that somewhere outside, her son is waiting to come home.

item.title: He survived Milestone. The pain didn’t
item.description:
When the fire was finally extinguished after the Bangladesh Air Force training aircraft crashed into Milestone School and College last July, six-year-old Kafi Ahmed Taif had survived.
A year later, survival remains only the beginning of his story.
The Class VI student still undergoes monthly hospital visits, laser therapy, physiotherapy and psychological counselling. His hands swell without treatment. Skin grafts continue to heal. The pain can become so intense during therapy that his father cannot bear to stay in the room.
For many of the children who escaped one of Bangladesh’s deadliest aviation disasters, recovery has become a second battle -- one fought not against flames, but against lifelong physical injuries, emotional trauma and mounting financial hardship.
Kafi’s father, Miraj Ahmed, still remembers the phone call that transformed an ordinary working day into a nightmare.
He had dropped his son at Milestone School and College in Uttara that morning before leaving for work in Dhanmondi.
Kafi’s mother later arrived with their younger daughter to collect him after class.
A teacher asked them to wait another 10 minutes because Kafi had been kept back.
Those 10 minutes changed everything.
While waiting near the school grounds, the Bangladesh Air Force FT-7 BGI training aircraft crashed into the campus.
Kafi was trapped inside his classroom.
His mother ran into the smoke-filled building searching for her son.
He was pulled out alive, but his face, ears, throat and both hands had suffered severe burns.
By the time Miraj Ahmed reached Uttara, his son had already been taken to Crescent Hospital before being transferred to the National Institute of Burn and Plastic Surgery.
“My son was writhing in pain in the ambulance,” he told Dhaka Tribune.
“Not just my child, I saw many other children suffering the same way.”
The horror deepened at the Burn Institute.
“Parents were screaming everywhere. Children had burns on their hands, legs, faces and heads. The smell of burnt flesh filled the hospital. I will never forget that.”
Doctors first spent 24 hours determining whether Kafi’s airway had been damaged.
Then came another anxious wait to determine whether his eyesight could be saved.
“I kept asking him what colour shirt I was wearing,” Miraj recalled. “When he answered correctly, I finally felt some relief.”
Kafi remained in hospital for more than two months.
Doctors performed skin grafts using tissue taken from his leg to rebuild both hands and operated on his right ear, eventually restoring his hearing.
But returning home did not mean the suffering had ended.
“The pain was unbearable,” his father said. “He would tell me, ‘Dad, it hurts so much. It would have been better if I had died.’ Sometimes he even talked about ending his own life.”
The family sought help from psychiatrists and clinical psychologists, while specialists at the Burn Institute began long-term counselling to help Kafi recover emotionally.
Even today, treatment continues.
Monthly follow-up appointments are accompanied by laser therapy, physiotherapy, massage and daily exercises. Without regular treatment, swelling returns to his hands and feet.
“When doctors bend his fingers during laser therapy, he screams in pain,” Miraj said. “I cannot watch. I leave the room. His mother stays beside him.”
Recovery has also brought a heavy financial burden.
Miraj estimates the family has already spent around Tk600,000 on medicines alone, despite receiving some support from the Burn Institute.
Many specialised medicines cost more than Tk3,000 for bottles that last only a few days.
During the early stages of recovery, doctors also prescribed a high-protein diet that significantly increased household expenses.
“I have another child to raise,” he said. “Whatever my son needs, I somehow arrange it.”
Apart from limited assistance from Prime Bank, he says the family has received little long-term institutional support.
Today Kafi has returned to Milestone School.
His parents considered transferring him elsewhere but decided against it.
They believe his teachers and classmates understand his condition in ways that a new school never could.
He attends classes mainly to rebuild confidence rather than academic performance.
One year after the Milestone tragedy, the aircraft is gone, the headlines have faded and investigations have been completed.
For Kafi, however, recovery is still measured not in months, but in hospital appointments, painful therapy sessions and the hope that one day life might finally feel normal again.

item.title: For Bappi’s family, July 21 never ended
item.description:
Nearly a year after the fighter jet crash at Milestone School and College claimed the life of eight-year-old Bappi, his mother Bithi says the loudest reminder of her son is not a photograph, a school bag or an empty bedroom -- it is the rhythmic beep of the life-support machine that echoed through the intensive care unit during his final hours.
She still hears it.
The sound has followed her every day since July 21, 2025, when the Bangladesh Air Force’s FT-7 BGI training aircraft crashed into the Uttara school campus, killing 36 people, including 28 students.
“When Bappi was on life support, I kept hearing that ‘beep... beep...’,” she told Dhaka Tribune, struggling to hold back tears.
“A year has passed, but that sound still rings in my ears. Sometimes I feel like I am standing in front of the ICU again.”
For Bappi’s parents, time has barely moved since that afternoon.
Every detail of their final morning together remains painfully clear.
Like every school day, Bappi’s mother woke before sunrise to prepare breakfast for her two sons.
Bappi, a Class III student, wanted chapati instead of the bread she had initially planned.
“I was going to make Horlicks,” she recalled. “Then he said, ‘Mom, why don’t you make chapati?’ So I made chicken chapati. He ate happily.”
Later that morning she packed his tiffin and headed to the school after dropping off his younger brother, Vijay, a nursery student.
Normally she would wait until Bappi’s class ended and feed him herself.
That day, the class was still in session.
She handed the lunchbox to a school nanny.
“I still don’t know whether my son ever ate the food I packed for him.”
Minutes later, a phone call shattered the ordinary morning.
“The plane has crashed at Milestone. Come immediately.”
She rushed back to the school, where panic had already consumed the campus.
Burned children were being carried out one after another.
She searched classrooms, corridors and open spaces but could not find Bappi.
“I kept telling myself I would find him alive.”
Her husband searched hospitals across the city until the family finally received a call from the National Institute of Burn and Plastic Surgery.
Inside the ICU, she recognised her son immediately.
“Others could not recognise him because of the burns,” she said. “But I am his mother. I knew it was Bappi.”
She remembers his face, hands and head covered with severe burns.
One memory has haunted her ever since.
“A few days earlier I had cut his hair short. Now I keep thinking if I had left it longer, maybe his head would not have burned so badly.”
The following morning, doctors called the family.
Before breaking the news, they asked Bappi’s father how many children he had.
“When they told me to stay strong, I understood my son was gone,” he recalled.
A year later, the family’s grief has evolved into unanswered questions.
They say they have never been shown CCTV footage from the school, never received the investigation report and still have no sense that anyone has been held accountable.
“We have only one demand,” Bappi’s mother said.
“We want justice.”
The tragedy also changed the life of Bappi’s younger brother.
After losing their eldest son, the family withdrew Vijay from Milestone and enrolled him elsewhere.
His mother says she still cannot bring herself to walk past the school where Bappi spent his final day.
“My legs stop moving whenever I go there,” she said.
“No amount of money can replace a child.”
Nearly a year after the disaster that shook the nation, official investigations have been completed, committees have submitted reports and recommendations have been issued.
But inside one family’s home, July 21 has never truly ended.
The last tiffin remains uneaten in memory.
The ICU monitor still echoes.
And a mother continues to wait -- not for her son to return, because she knows he never will -- but for the justice she believes never arrived.

item.title: Iran envoy: Culture and faith were our strongest weapons
item.description:
The Iranian Cultural Counselor in Dhaka has said Iran’s ability to withstand its recent conflict with the United States and Israel was rooted as much in its history, cultural identity and religious faith as in its military capabilities, while calling for stronger media and cultural cooperation between Bangladesh and Iran during a visit to the Dhaka Tribune office.
During an exchange of views with Dhaka Tribune Editor Reaz Ahmad and senior journalists on Monday, Iranian Cultural Counselor Mahdi Molaee Arani discussed the recent regional conflict, Iran’s domestic response, the role of national identity in times of war, and the importance of media in promoting mutual understanding between nations.
The meeting also focused on expanding cooperation between Bangladesh and Iran beyond diplomacy.
Both sides agreed in principle to pursue knowledge exchange, media collaboration, and joint initiatives to promote each country’s history, cultural heritage and tourism.
They also stressed that responsible journalism can play an important role in strengthening people-to-people ties and countering misconceptions between nations.
Speaking about the recent conflict, Molaee said many international observers had attempted to explain Iran’s resilience primarily through military strength.
In his view, however, such an explanation overlooks the country’s deeper social and cultural foundations.
“Many people ask how Iran managed to stand firm against two of the world’s most powerful military forces after losing some of its senior military commanders,” he said.
“The answer cannot be found only in military capability.”
According to Molaee, many international media outlets portrayed ordinary Iranians as fearful and demoralized during the conflict.
He argued that the reality inside the country was markedly different.
“In many wars, people flee, governments relocate and society descends into panic,” he said.
“In Iran, we witnessed the opposite. Many Iranians living abroad returned home in solidarity, and people worked alongside rescue teams and security personnel instead of abandoning their communities.”
The Iranian envoy said this resilience stemmed from what he described as the country’s “soft power” -- its history, culture, national identity and faith.
He noted that Iran’s late Supreme Leader often distinguished between hard power and soft power, arguing that while military capability is essential for national defence, a nation’s long-term endurance depends on the strength of its people, their historical consciousness and their shared beliefs.
Molaee said Iran’s historical experience had reinforced that understanding.
Referring to the country’s occupation during the World War II despite declaring neutrality, he said Iranians had learned that weapons alone cannot guarantee sovereignty.
Religion, he added, has also played a defining role in shaping public resilience.
Citing Quranic teachings on standing firmly for truth and justice, he said many Iranians believe that numerical or military superiority does not ultimately determine the outcome of conflicts.
“We believe that those who sacrifice their lives for truth do not truly die,” he said.
“This belief gives people strength during the most difficult moments.”
Molaee also highlighted the contribution of Persian literature to Iran’s national identity, describing Abul Qasem Ferdowsi’s* epic Shahnama as a cornerstone of Iranian cultural consciousness.
He said the work continues to inspire patriotism, unity and self-sacrifice across generations, adding that Bangladesh and Iran share centuries of historical and cultural interaction.
Responding to questions about the possibility of renewed hostilities, Molaee said Iran does not regard war as a solution and continues to favour what he described as a “just and dignified peace.”
However, he maintained that peace imposed through external pressure would not be sustainable.
“The principles of independence, sovereignty and national dignity are not negotiable,” he said.
Concluding the discussion, Molaee reiterated that Iran’s resilience should not be viewed solely through the lens of military capability.
“A nation that remains connected to its history, culture and identity cannot be easily defeated,” he said.
The meeting ended with both sides expressing optimism that greater cooperation between the media of Bangladesh and Iran could contribute to a deeper understanding of each other’s societies while promoting shared historical, cultural and tourism links.

item.title: Milestone tragedy: Risk still flies over Uttara
item.description:
One year after a Bangladesh Air Force training aircraft crashed into Milestone School and College, killing 36 people, including 28 students, Bangladesh’s aviation safety overhaul has largely stalled, with hundreds of hazardous buildings still standing around Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport despite repeated official directives to remove them.
A Dhaka Tribune investigation has found that many of the key safety measures ordered after the July 21, 2025 disaster remain either partially implemented or entirely unfulfilled, raising fresh concerns over whether Bangladesh has acted on the lessons of one of its worst aviation tragedies.
In a significant admission, RAJUK Chairman Engineer Md Reazul Islam Rizu acknowledged that authorities have made no visible progress in removing many of the dangerous structures identified around the airport corridor.
He said RAJUK has identified 630 buildings that potentially violate aviation safety restrictions between 2015 and 2025, but legal proceedings, eviction drives and enforcement actions remain incomplete in most cases.
“Even one year after the Milestone tragedy, visible progress in removing hazardous buildings around the airport has not been achieved,” the chairman told Dhaka Tribune.
He also acknowledged that political and administrative influence has obstructed enforcement efforts.
“Political and administrative pressure has become a barrier in implementing some eviction activities,” he said.
The admission is one of the clearest official acknowledgements to date that institutional obstacles, not merely technical challenges, have prevented authorities from implementing reforms promised after the disaster.
The chairman also disclosed that disagreements between RAJUK and the Civil Aviation Authority of Bangladesh (CAAB) over technical data have delayed the joint field survey needed to verify building heights around airport approach and departure corridors.
According to him, the planned removal of structures located within the mandatory 300-foot safety buffer beside the Metro Rail depot has also failed to progress as intended.
Internal RAJUK documents reviewed by Dhaka Tribune show that authorities ordered an extensive package of emergency reforms immediately after the crash.
These included demolishing unsafe structures around the Milestone campus, clearing the Metro Rail safety buffer, identifying buildings exceeding airport height restrictions, enforcing approved land-use plans, shutting unauthorized hostel operations, ensuring compliance with the Bangladesh National Building Code 2020, and preparing an Air Funnel Zone policy to control future development near airport flight paths.
Yet field visits found that although portions of the crash-damaged building have been demolished, many surrounding structures identified as safety concerns remain untouched.
A senior RAJUK official, speaking on condition of anonymity, described the situation as an institutional failure.
“There is no scope for RAJUK to avoid responsibility,” the official said.
“Seven or eight coordination meetings have been held since the tragedy, but we have not reached an effective operational conclusion.”
RAJUK Director (Planning) Ashraful Islam similarly acknowledged that many decisions remain at the planning stage.
“We are taking steps on all issues, but many of them are still in planning,” he said.
The investigation also found that despite the existence of the list of 630 allegedly non-compliant buildings, authorities could not provide a comprehensive public record showing how many have been demolished, regularized, fined or cleared after inspection.
The absence of a transparent enforcement database has further fuelled questions about regulatory accountability.
Urban planning experts warn that the delay increases future risks.
BUET Professor Hadiuzzaman said airport funnel zones require strict protection under international aviation standards and cautioned that policy discussions alone cannot prevent future disasters.
Bangladesh Institute of Planners General Secretary Sk Mehdi Hasan said the Milestone tragedy reflects a familiar pattern in Bangladesh.
“A major accident occurs, committees are formed, recommendations are issued, agencies become active for a short period, and then momentum fades,” he said.
Victims’ families also questioned why responsibility continues to shift between institutions while many of the underlying hazards remain.
The Milestone crash investigation concluded that pilot error caused the accident, but it also found serious deficiencies in the school’s infrastructure, including non-compliance with building safety requirements that investigators said contributed to the high casualty toll.
One year later, however, the broader reforms intended to make the airport corridor safer remain unfinished.
The Air Funnel Zone policy has yet to be finalised, the joint height survey has not begun, the Metro Rail safety buffer has not been fully cleared, and hundreds of buildings identified by regulators continue to await legal action.
The Milestone disaster exposed critical weaknesses in Bangladesh’s aviation and urban planning oversight.
A year later, the investigation suggests the state’s biggest challenge is no longer identifying the risks, but enforcing the rules designed to eliminate them.

item.title: Allies voice frustration over lack of recognition at PM meeting
item.description:
Leaders of political parties allied with the BNP during the anti-government movement voiced frustration at a meeting with Prime Minister and BNP Chairman Tarique Rahman on Monday, saying they have not received due recognition since the BNP assumed power.
They said their parties had been valued during the joint movement but claimed the BNP has since adopted a "go-it-alone" approach. The leaders also called for greater representation of coalition partners in the government and state institutions.
The meeting, followed by a dinner, was held at the state guest house Jamuna in Dhaka. It marked the first formal meeting between Prime Minister Tarique Rahman and leaders of the BNP's alliance partners since the BNP-led government took office.
According to multiple participants, discussions centred on the government's first five months in office, the role of coalition partners in the administration, growing strains within the alliance, and the government's overall performance. Although more than 100 leaders attended, only a limited number were given the opportunity to speak.
Saiful Haque, leader of the Democratic Platform (Gonotantra Mancha) and general secretary of the Revolutionary Workers Party of Bangladesh, said neither the BNP nor the government had held any formal meeting with its allies during the past five months. He alleged that coalition leaders were being sidelined at various levels of government despite having played an equal role in the anti-government movement.
Nagorik Oikya President Mahmudur Rahman Manna, however, praised several of the government's development initiatives and public welfare measures. Abu Hanif, a senior leader of the Gono Odhikar Parishad, said alliance leaders raised both longstanding grievances and current concerns with the prime minister. According to Hanif, Tarique Rahman listened attentively and assured them that their contributions would receive due recognition.
Participants said the demand for meaningful representation of coalition partners in the administration featured prominently in the discussions. Several leaders also complained that the BNP's dominance at the grassroots level was straining relations within the alliance.
Leaders of several Islamic parties attending the dinner alleged that while left-leaning and younger politicians had been accommodated in the cabinet, parties representing Islamic values had been overlooked.
Maulana Azizul Haque Islamabadi, joint secretary general of Hefazat-e-Islam Bangladesh, said his organisation, despite being a significant Islamic force, had not received the recognition it deserved. He added that the lack of inclusive participation in governance had disappointed the party's leaders and activists.
Before taking office, the BNP regularly met its alliance partners during the three-year joint movement against the Awami League government. Monday's gathering was the first formal meeting since the new government was formed.
Nearly 50 political parties joined the BNP in the anti-government movement. Ahead of the 13th parliamentary election, the BNP left several constituencies for its allies.
Representatives from the Democratic Platform, Gono Odhikar Parishad and the National Democratic Movement (NDM) are currently serving in the government.
According to BNP sources, around 150 leaders from allied and like-minded parties were invited to the meeting. However, two key allies, the Jamiat Ulema-e-Islam Bangladesh and the Jatiya Samajtantrik Dal (JSD), did not attend.
JSD Senior Vice-President Tania Rob confirmed that the party had received the prime minister's invitation but declined to participate. She said the party had also sent a written response explaining the reasons for its decision.

item.title: Kaikobad requests Saudi govt to retain 1pc backup accommodation for Bangladesh Pilgrims
item.description:
Religious Affairs Minister Kazi Shah Mofazzal Houssain Kaikobad on Monday requested the Saudi government to retain the backup accommodation quota for Bangladesh at one percent for the 2027 Hajj, instead of increasing it.
The minister made the request while paying a courtesy call to Saudi Arabian Ambassador to Bangladesh Dr Abdullah Jafar H Bin Abiyah at the Saudi Embassy in Gulshan on Monday afternoon.
The Saudi Ministry of Hajj and Umrah has fixed the backup accommodation quota at 2% for the 2027 Hajj.
The increase would raise the overall cost of Hajj, therefore, the minister requested that Bangladesh's backup accommodation quota be maintained at 1% like before.
The Saudi ambassador said he had received a semi-official letter from the Ministry of Religious Affairs on the matter yesterday and had forwarded it to the Saudi government with his recommendation.
He also praised Bangladesh's Hajj management this year and expressed satisfaction with the Ministry of Religious Affairs' prompt action on all bilateral matters.
The letter from the Ministry requests the Saudi govt to keep catering optional and fix the service charge for Service Package-3 at a level corresponding to the value of Service Package 'D' for services in Mina and Arafah.
The minister thanked the ambassador for his role in Bangladesh's Hajj management this year.
He also thanked the Saudi government for ensuring smooth, orderly and well-organized overall Hajj management.
During the meeting, the two sides discussed the issues of mutual interest.
Earlier, the ambassador warmly received the religion minister upon his arrival at the Saudi Embassy.

item.title: Rizvi: Key issues need consensus to protect democracy
item.description:
BNP Senior Joint Secretary General Ruhul Kabir Rizvi on Monday said democracy could once again come under threat if political parties fail to maintain a minimum level of mutual understanding on key national issues.
He said: "Political parties must collectively maintain at least a minimum understanding on some fundamental national issues. If they fail to do so, democracy will once again be endangered. Along with democracy, the country's independence and sovereignty could also be put at risk."
He was speaking at a discussion at the auditorium of the International University of Business Agriculture and Technology (IUBAT).
Rizvi alleged that the previous "fascist" government systematically dismantled democratic institutions, including the Election Commission, judiciary, and media, to remain in power indefinitely.
He said: "All democratic institutions were destroyed. The judiciary had no independence, the Election Commission became a tool for staging farcical elections and the media was tightly controlled. This is how fascist regimes operate everywhere."
He said opposition political parties were subjected to repression, citing the imprisonment of BNP Chairperson Khaleda Zia under harsh conditions as part of an effort to weaken the opposition.
Recalling the July uprising, Rizvi said the painful memories of those days remain vivid.
He said the July-August movement had restored some democratic space by ensuring conditions for a free and fair election and allowing people to criticize the government without fear of enforced disappearance or extrajudicial killing.
He said: "In a democratic society, people must be able to speak and criticize freely. That was absent before. The July movement restored that right. Its significance is therefore profound."
He called for further discussions between the government and political parties on the July Charter, saying any remaining issues should be resolved through dialogue.

item.title: HC issues rule to bar political figures from private school governing bodies
item.description:
The High Court on Monday issued a rule asking why individuals affiliated with political parties or holding political positions should not be declared ineligible for election, nomination or approval to the governing bodies and managing committees of private educational institutions by amending the existing regulations or framing new ones.
The court also sought an explanation as to why legal provisions should not be introduced to ensure the inclusion of locally respected education enthusiasts, retired teachers, persons of integrity and repute, freedom fighters, educationists, lawyers, physicians and other distinguished citizens in these committees. It further asked why judicial guidelines should not be issued in this regard.
The rule was issued by a High Court bench of Justice Ahmed Sohel and Justice Fatema Anwar after hearing a writ petition.
Advocates Md Nadir Khan and Md Sohel Rana represented the petitioner.
The writ was filed on June 7 in the public interest by Advocate Md Nadir Khan on behalf of a guardian, Rubel Mia.
The petition sought an amendment to Rule 7 of the Private Educational Institutions Governing Bodies and Managing Committees Regulations, 2024 , or the formulation of a new uniform regulation applicable to all education boards.
According to the petition, allowing individuals affiliated with political parties or holding party positions to serve on governing bodies and managing committees could compromise the neutrality, accountability and good governance of private educational institutions. It therefore urged the authorities to enact the necessary legal provisions to ensure the participation of respected, honest and education-minded members of society in these committees.

item.title: PM exchanges greetings with leaders of allied political parties
item.description:
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman on Monday exchanged greetings with leaders of the political parties that participated in the simultaneous anti-fascist movement at State Guest House Jamuna in Dhaka on Monday evening.
The prime minister arrived at the venue in the open courtyard of the State Guest House at 7:27 pm, where arrangements had been made for the leaders of the parties that took part in the joint movement.
Tarique Rahman went from table to table, exchanging greetings with the leaders of the allied leaders. He was accompanied by BNP Secretary General and LGRD and Cooperatives Mirza Fakhrul Islam Alamgir.
Later, the formal program began at 7:40 pm with the recitation of the Holy Quran.
Leaders of 41 political parties that had participated in the movement to oust the fascist government were invited to the event.
Members of the BNP Standing Committee and members of the liaison committee formed during the movement joined the event.
This is the first formal meeting between Prime Minister Tarique Rahman and the leaders of the parties allied in the anti-fascist movement since the BNP formed the government after securing a majority in the 13th parliamentary election held on February 12.
Among those invited were leaders of the Ganatantra Mancha, the 12-Party Alliance, the Like-Minded Nationalist Alliance, the Democratic Left Alliance, Islami Oikya Jote, and other Islamic political parties.

item.title: Three more children die with measles symptoms in Sylhet
item.description:
Three more children died of measles symptoms in Sylhet in the last 24 hours, raising the death toll from measles and measles-like symptoms in the division to 103.
The three children died while undergoing treatment at Sylhet MAG Osmani Medical College Hospital, Sylhet Divisional Office of Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS) said on Monday.
Assistant Director of Sylhet Health Department Dr Noor-e-Alam said two of the deceased children, both under the age of two, were from Sunamganj, while the other was from Habiganj. Of the 103 victims who have died so far in Sylhet division, one was an adult and the rest were children.
Sunamganj has recorded the highest number of deaths in the division, with 47 children losing their lives so far. Besides, 35 deaths were reported in Sylhet, 12 in Moulvibazar and nine in Habiganj.
Meanwhile, 265 patients with measles symptoms are currently undergoing treatment at different hospitals across Sylhet Division.
According to the health department, a total of 534 laboratory-confirmed measles cases have been identified in the division since January 1, 2026. In the last 24 hours, 57 more patients with measles symptoms have been admitted to hospitals in Sylhet.
Authorities at Sylhet MAG Osmani Medical College Hospital said all-out efforts are being made to ensure proper treatment for patients. A total of 20 ICU beds have been set up at Osmani Medical College Hospital and 14 at Shaheed Shamsuddin Ahmed Hospital.

item.title: Journalist Saidur Rahman appointed press minister to New Delhi
item.description:
The government has appointed Md Saidur Rahman, a journalist at The Daily Ittefaq, as press minister at the Bangladesh High Commission in New Delhi, India.
A notification issued by the Ministry of Public Administration on Monday said he has been appointed for a 1-year term from the date of joining, subject to relinquishing all professional engagements, businesses, and positions with any government, semi-government, private institution, or other organization.
Saidur Rahman earned both his bachelor's and master's degrees from the Department of Mass Communication and Journalism at the University of Dhaka.
He began his journalism career as the University of Dhaka correspondent for Dainik Dinkal before joining The Daily Ittefaq.
Following the July Movement, he was promoted to the position of Politics and Election Editor at The Daily Ittefaq.
He previously served as general secretary of the Dhaka University Journalists' Association and as president of the Reporters Forum for Election and Democracy (RFED), an organization of journalists covering the Election Commission.

item.title: Jamuna erosion intensifies in Bogra as rising waters devour homes, cropland
item.description:
River erosion along the Jamuna River has intensified in Dhunat upazila of Bogra amid rising water levels caused by heavy rainfall and upstream inflows, leaving residents fearful of losing their homes, farmland and livelihoods.
Local residents say the erosion is moving closer to the flood control embankment, heightening concerns among thousands living along the riverbanks.
According to the Bogra Water Development Board (BWDB), the Jamuna's water level reached 15.57 metres on Saturday morning, rising nine centimetres over the previous 24 hours. Although the river remains 68 centimetres below the danger mark, water levels continue to increase.
Field visits to the affected areas found strong currents and whirlpools eroding riverbanks at an alarming rate. Farmland, trees and homesteads are being swallowed by the river as sections of soil collapse into the water.
The worst-hit area is a roughly 200-metre stretch between Shaharbari and Baniajan villages, where fresh land is disappearing into the river almost every day.
Farmers including Jewel Sheikh, Mizanur Rahman, Ziaul Haque and Asad Sheikh said they had already lost their homes and several bighas of farmland.
“Everything is disappearing before our eyes,” they said. “Within days, our land and houses have been washed away. If the erosion continues, Shaharbari village could one day disappear from the map.”
Residents alleged that despite severe erosion occurring almost every monsoon, no permanent river protection measures have been put in place. They warned that continued erosion could eventually threaten the flood control embankment.
BWDB Sub-Assistant Engineer Abdul Malek said increased pressure from upstream flows had triggered erosion in several riverside locations.
“Emergency protection work is underway using sand-filled geo-bags and tube dumping to curb the erosion,” he said.

item.title: Bhaluka MP named in attacks, lawsuits, and takeover attempts
item.description:
After the July uprising, allegations of attempts to occupy various industrial establishments and involvement in extortion activities in Bhaluka,

Mymensingh were leveled against local BNP leader Fakhruddin Ahmed, also known as Bacchu. At that time, he was expelled from the party.

A central BNP joint secretary general filed a case against him during that period.

However, within a year, Fakhruddin Ahmed was acquitted from the case. Alongside, he was elected as a Member of Parliament from Mymensingh-11 constituency (Bhaluka Upazila) in the 13th National Parliamentary Election on BNP's nomination. Now, he is also the convener of the Bhaluka Upazila BNP. After being elected as a Member of Parliament, Fakhruddin's name comes up again regarding attacks, lawsuits against party opponents, and controlling the jhoot business.

On Saturday (18July), the central BNP issued a show cause notice to Member of Parliament Fakhruddin for allegedly engaging in various unethical and malevolent activities, breaching party discipline. The notice, signed by the party's senior joint secretary general Ruhul Kabir Rizvi, demanded a written explanation from Fakhruddin.

Earlier, on 14 June , former joint convener of Bhaluka Upazila Chhatra Dal Sharif Hasan brought allegations against this Member of Parliament to BNP's Chairman and Prime Minister Tarique Rahman. He alleged that on 13 June, the Member of Parliament's followers attacked them as they were participating in a conference of upazila and municipal Chhatra Dal at the MP's behest.

The complaint to the Prime Minister stated that since the parliamentary election, Fakhruddin Ahmed has been trying to expand his empire individually. If there was any dissent, he would resort to various attacks and torture on the party's tested leaders and workers. Moreover, he has been arresting and harassing party leaders and activists in false cases.

Chhatra Dal leader Sharif Hasan, who brought the allegations against the Member of Parliament, told Prothom Alo, "A situation has been created where no political activities can be conducted. Out of fear of attacks, open conversations or just hanging out is not possible. "

On 3 March, Mizanur Rahman, a member of the Habirbari union Jubo Dal in Bhaluka, filed a written complaint with the Deputy Inspector General of Police of Mymensingh Range, mentioning several incidents of attack, vandalism, and looting by the MP's followers.

The written complaint stated that despite being attacked, the police station does not accept any case. Such a situation has led locals in Bhaluka to lose faith in the local police administration.

In the written complaint, Mizanur mentioned that on 1 March, an attack, vandalism, and looting were carried out at his home. He also referred several incidents, including an attack and vandalism at the home of former joint convener of Bhaluka Municipal Swechchhasebok Dal, Tias Mahmud, on 23 February.

Regarding the matter, Tias Mahmud told Prothom Alo, "During the last election, Fakhruddin's personal force attacked us for working for an independent candidate. Even though a complaint was taken to the police station, no case was filed, which is why a complaint was submitted to the DIG. When summoned, we provided a written statement. However, no action has yet been taken regarding our complaint."

Conflict over jhoot business

There are 155 factories listed by the industrial police in the industrial area of Bhaluka, Mymensingh, with 145 currently operational. Unused fabric and yarn from different factories are sold separately, known as the ''jhoot business.''

Multiple sources in Bhaluka Upazila BNP say that after the July uprising, the jhoot business of most industrial establishments in Bhaluka went under the control of the then joint convener of the Upazila BNP, Muhammad Morshed Alam's subordinates.

He was expelled from BNP for becoming a ''rebel'' candidate in the last parliamentary elections. After Fakhruddin Ahmed became a Member of Parliament on BNP's nomination, his followers tried to take control of the jhoot business of the industrial factories, leading to a conflict between the two groups.

Habirbari union in Bhaluka has the most industrial factories. Md Shahjahan Khan, a member of this union council and former general secretary of Ward No. 2 BNP, told Prothom Alo that while Morshed's group previously managed the jhoot business, now the MP's subordinates are trying to take control. This control and sharing of profits have led to conflicts between the two groups.

Hijacking of factory trucks

The factory of Envoy Textiles Limited, a leading denim (jeans) manufacturing company in the country, is located in Bhaluka. On 11 July, they applied for security to the industrial police in Bhaluka.

The application made by Md Sarwar Hossain, Deputy General Manager of the administration department of Envoy Textiles Limited, stated that on 9 July, at noon, a truck carrying empty chemical drums used by Envoy Textiles Limited was hijacked forcefully from in front of the main gate of the factory. Immediately after the incident, governmental agencies and law enforcement were informed. That night, the truck was recovered by the industrial police.

Later, it was discovered that Md Ibrahim Khalil, former assistant organisational secretary of Mymensingh South District Swechchhasebok Dal, Md Sohag Miah, a union-level leader of the Swechchhasebok Dal, and others were involved in the hijacking of the truck. They openly threatened not to let the jhoot out from the factory. Moreover, they have been preventing sand, crushed stone, and other materials used in the construction of Envoy Textiles from entering the factory, causing construction work to come to a halt.

Multiple leaders of Bhaluka Upazila BNP told Prothom Alo that Ibrahim Khalil and Sohag Miah are followers of the local Member of Parliament.

Acknowledging the incident of holding back Envoy Textiles’ truck, the current police superintendent of Bhaluka industrial police, Md Ansar Uddin, told Prothom Alo that initially, the representatives of the institution tried to resolve the issue locally by talking to the Member of Parliament, but it was not resolved. Later, they sought assistance from the industrial police.

After contacting those named in the complaint, the truck was returned intact by the evening, and the institution's authorities stated they had received the materials and were not interested in filing a case.

Business interference

Multiple local BNP sources state that Morshed Alam, expelled from the party for being a rebel candidate, has been running the jhoot business in SQ Group’s Colour Master factory and other establishments in Jamirdia area of Bhaluka for about 22 years.

On 4 July, HRKM Enterprise, owned by him, tried to get jhoot materials out from that factory. At that time, the MP's followers obstructed them, leading to tension in the area. Additional police were deployed there to control the situation.

Morshed Alam told Prothom Alo, "Since the last parliamentary election, the people loyal to the local MP have been obstructing my business aggressively. Following the MP’s instruction, I was named in two false cases. My leaders and activists are being harassed and falsely implicated in cases, forcing them to leave the area. "

I have no subordinates

However, Member of Parliament Fakhruddin Ahmed denied all allegations. Last Monday evening, he told Prothom Alo, "I was not in any position in the party even during the election. My expulsion order was withdrawn, and I was nominated for the election. I won with the highest margin in Mymensingh district. I have no subordinates, as none of my brothers, friends, or relatives are involved in business. Those who claim my subordinates are here are instigated by a malicious circle. These are propaganda spread by those who have long collaborated with fascists and had business ties with them to hold BNP leaders and activists responsible."

The central BNP had given 48 hours to respond to the show cause notice given to the Member of Parliament last Saturday. MP Fakhruddin mentioned that he had responded to the notice.

When asked why such allegations of attack, lawsuit, and attempt to occupy factories are repeatedly coming up, this Member of Parliament said, "No factory owner has made any complaint against me yet. No one can say that I have sent anyone directly to any factory, gone myself, or any brother, friend, or relative of mine has gone. "

Fakhruddin was expelled from BNP for breaching party discipline on 1 September 2024. The next day, BNP joint secretary general Syed Emran Saleh (Prince) filed a case against him with Bhaluka police station following party decision. He is now also the administrator of Mymensingh District Council.

Syed Emran Saleh, in a phone conversation with Prothom Alo last night, said that the party high command's viewpoint will undeniably be strict regarding any unethical or illegal work.
